video_title: "We're in an Era of Agent-to-Agent War." Index Ventures on AI & Cybersecurity
gist: Index Ventures partner Shardul Shah (Sourcery with Molly O'Shea) describes Index's people-first, anti-pattern approach to investing, why price matters little within ~25%, the 'luxury product effect' of high valuations on hiring, and M&A/IPO exits. Despite the title's cybersecurity/agent-to-agent war framing, security gets only brief treatment (public security companies approaching ~$1T, a bet on a clean-sheet security platform); the conversation is mostly VC philosophy and firm background.

insights.claim: Index backs people before ideas: it invested in Waze before a business plan, market or metrics existed, and in several young AI founders (Flapping Airplanes, Simile, Cartesia) before the founder knew what they would build. There is no thematic or age screen.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Early-stage AI selection is a bet on founder quality, so thematic 'coverage' maps are a weak predictor of which seed checks Index writes.
insights.quote: we weren't targeting 26 and under founders

insights.claim: Shah explicitly rejects pattern-matching founder filters; his stated screen is 'duality' (creative plus operationally detailed), which he argues produces adaptability when model capabilities change every few months.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: In a market where retention and durability shift quarterly, adaptability is the trait he is underwriting rather than any fixed business model.

insights.claim: Shah says what is 'durable' is hard to assess because model capabilities emerge every few months; what is retentive today may not be tomorrow, so durability assessment itself is shifting with the market.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Moat analysis for AI startups is unstable; investors lean on founder adaptability instead of retention metrics.

insights.claim: Sometimes entrepreneurs confuse revenue with a durable business model in an environment where abundance brings exuberance.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Fast AI revenue ramps deserve scrutiny for churn and substitution risk.

insights.claim: Hardest part of winning deals is conviction/connection with the founder, not price; Index is an equal partnership with little credit-taking, which lets whichever partner connects best lead, then the firm moves fast and aggressively.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Speed of decision once conviction exists is a competitive lever against better-marketed mega funds.

themes.theme: Price, Capital and the Luxury-Product Effect

insights.claim: Shah argues more capital is flowing into a finite set of private-market outcomes, so prices 'are high' and 'will get higher'; he calls this basic supply and demand.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: A mega-fund GP is publicly underwriting continued valuation inflation in private tech.

insights.claim: Index's admitted 'sin of omission' is being 'cute on price' (e.g., GitHub): being ~25% off on price doesn't matter, but being 2x off signals someone believes something Index doesn't and warrants inspection.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Rule of thumb: pay up within ~25% for category-defining companies; larger gaps are a signal to re-examine thesis.

insights.claim: Counterintuitively, a higher valuation and larger raise make it easier for a startup to recruit talent: a 'luxury product effect' where high price signals scarcity, defying the arithmetic that lower strike prices favor employees.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Down-pricing a round to be 'fair' can hurt hiring; founders may rationally prefer headline price.

insights.claim: Check sizes range from about $1M to over $100M; Index will not run a statistical game of thousands of $1M checks because it can't follow through with real engagement. It keeps 30-35 investments in a venture portfolio and invested over $250M into Wiz across funds.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Concentration is moderated but unbounded per name; Shah warns concentration cuts both ways if the market turns.

insights.claim: Industry pacing accelerated over the last 12 months with more deals and larger dollars, compressing the ~2.5 year fund cycle; Shah expects a probable return to normal but says Index prefers vintage diversification.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Faster fund-raising cadence across the industry is an AI-era artifact that may revert.

insights.claim: M&A has accelerated and includes private-to-private deals; Shah cites Wiz, Cursor and World Labs as examples, while the IPO window is outside investors' control.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Liquidity for venture is increasingly coming through strategic and private-to-private transactions rather than IPOs.

insights.claim: Reported performance: 11x DPI on Index's 2012 fund versus an industry average of 1.5x, and 5.1x DPI on a $780M growth fund raised in 2015 (as of January 2026, per Bloomberg as cited by the host). Shah cautions against confusing outcomes with judgment quality.
insights.speaker: Molly O'Shea (host)
insights.so_what: Index DPI figures are outliers vs the 1.5x average; figures come from the host citing a press report, not Shah.

insights.claim: Whether to sell is a judgment call 'where there is no truth': the Adallom founders said no to Google once and later accepted; Wiz sold early or not is debatable, and Shah recalls partners calling when the stock rose after selling at the IPO price and not when it later fell.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Investor influence on sell-vs-stay decisions is where most shareholder value is created or lost.

insights.claim: Shah believes public-market security companies are approaching roughly $1T of combined value, calls the category permanent, and argues a clean-sheet platform that converges budgets (a company transcribed as '70 I', co-invested with Greylock) can rewrite the foundations in a way not possible 5-10 years ago.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Security vendor consolidation and platform replacement remains a venture-backed theme; incumbents' safety-by-brand appeals to some buyers.

insights.claim: Enterprise sales velocity is escalating: in the last six months Shah has seen a company sell $5M-$15M per year contracts within the first year of commercialization, faster than Wiz's record-setting ramp.
insights.speaker: Shardul Shah
insights.so_what: Benchmarks for 'fastest growing' are being reset by AI-native enterprise vendors.
